title: Italian Olympic Posters
excerpt: Two figures carry one another in a gestural composition that seems almost audible, the labored breath of ascent against the incline of a winter hillside.
body:
Two figures carry one another in a gestural composition that seems almost audible, the labored breath of ascent against the incline of a winter hillside. The image has the lived experience of Olympic athletes, its physicality rendered through sweeping, kinetic strokes. There is a vivacity here, a distinctly Italian sense of play and dynamism translated into two dimensions. The forms seem to pulse and unfurl, as if caught mid-creation, embodying both motion and spirit. In the context of the Olympic tradition, ancient in origin yet continually reimagined, these posters articulate strength, endurance, and movement with striking immediacy. Though the Olympic Games began in Greece, the Paralympic movement found early grounding in Rome in 1950, lending these works an added sense of return, of cultural homecoming.

Housed within the Italian Cultural Institute of Prague in the heart of Malá Strana, the exhibition unfolds with understated elegance. Visitors are welcomed at reception before being directed to the second floor, where the posters line a long corridor. This architectural framing enhances their impact. The elongated hallway mirrors the expansiveness of the Olympic ethos, while windows opening onto the courtyard invite shifting natural light to animate the works. On brighter days, sunlight filters across the surfaces, heightening their chromatic intensity and lending a quiet intimacy to the viewing experience. Beyond the display, a compact yet thoughtfully curated Italian library awaits, an extension of the cultural dialogue initiated by the posters themselves.

Among the works, one poster depicts two athletes at the conclusion of competition, bodies leaning into one another in mutual support. It is a quietly powerful image, underscoring solidarity amid rivalry. Another adopts a more whimsical tone, transforming the Olympic rings into scoops of gelato perched atop a cone, a playful nod to Italian culinary heritage. Elsewhere, compositions evoke the abstract dynamism of Futurism alongside gestures reminiscent of Wassily Kandinsky, with sharp, directional lines suggesting the velocity of downhill skiing. One particularly striking piece recalls mid-century aesthetics, its elongated figures clad in ski masks descending upon a vaulted cathedral. Another continues this gestural vitality, inscribed with the phrase, “Cracking the limit just like snowdrops crack cold ice,” a poetic invocation of resilience and transformation.

The breadth of work presented along this corridor might easily be overlooked, yet it’s worth it to stop on by. Each poster offers a distinct interpretive lens on the Olympic ideal, refracting themes of motion, unity, and perseverance. Collectively, they affirm the capacity of graphic art to encapsulate not only athletic spectacle but also the deeper human impulses that animate it.

images.alt: Two athletes in green, yellow and red support one another in a gestural Olympic poster.

title: Václav Benedikt at Toyen Gallery
excerpt: A yellow horse with red markings carries a quirky passenger who could be one of the friends of Donnie Darko.
body:
A yellow horse with red markings carries a quirky passenger who could be one of the friends of Donnie Darko. The image is one of the many paintings greeting visitors at Toyen Gallery in Václav Benedikt’s exhibition. The works are laced with hidden meanings and bursts of color that push into the sunlight of reality. Benedikt blends surrealism with a contemporary sensibility, creating paintings that invite viewers to look again later, wondering what they might have missed the first time.

In “Tajná jízda” (“Secret Ride”), the horse appears to have two heads and becomes a central metaphor. The dual heads suggest confusion and a lack of direction. The rider faces left, hinting that a choice may eventually be made. Beneath the horse is a field of blue that evokes water and movement, suggesting the need to follow the current when a path forward seems uncertain. Inside the yellow body of the horse sits a smaller black horse, possibly symbolizing youth or an inner voice guiding the journey. Meaning continues to build through texture, iconography, and color. “Torzo v modré” resembles a sewing machine, layered with the three-dimensional texture of a pocket. Blues dominate the composition, framed by a white cloud outline and thin red lines with an X marking the spot. The painting reads like a tribute to the labor and creativity it takes to turn fabric into something wearable.

“Duchovní spojení” continues the cloudlike ambiguity. Shapes drift through fields of blue and white punctuated by red marks. Some lines appear drawn by finger rather than brush, giving the work a visceral quality. The more one searches for meaning, the more the forms resist clarity, and that confusion draws the viewer further in. In “Žně,” blocks of brown and yellow with hints of green recall the landscapes of Paul Cézanne. The flattened space also evokes wide prairie plains. Bright colors remain balanced by soft whites and yellows that temper the composition. “Pomerančová krajina” suggests heat rising from beneath the earth’s surface. The imagery can be likened to the geological forces depicted in the video for Mutual Core by Björk, where pressure builds until it breaks through the surface. The final piece, “Inspirace modrou,” resembles an iceberg shaped like a human heart composed of faceted surfaces.

There are also several lithographs throughout the exhibition. Unlike the canvases, they feel sharper and more deliberate in their construction. The lines appear more controlled and graphic, and the colors sit apart from one another rather than blending into layered fields. This shift in medium introduces a different rhythm within the show, momentarily grounding the viewer before returning to the more fluid language of the paintings.

The exhibition ultimately feels like stepping into someone’s dreams. As with dreams, the details fade upon waking and must be pieced together again through fragments and impressions. Benedikt’s paintings leave viewers wanting to return, to look again, and to continue searching for what might still be hidden beneath the surface.

images.alt: A yellow horse and a pale masked rider against a blue background in a painting by Václav Benedikt.

title: Baroque Chapel at IIC
excerpt: An upside-down penny tails up is affixed to a page nested in dense swirling marks.
body:
An upside-down penny tails up is affixed to a page nested in dense swirling marks. Nearby, an ominous figure and an outstretched hand appear to beckon, whether summoning the coin or the viewer remains unclear. Is the penny a sign of luck, or its inverse? In the hands of Mario and Marisa Merz, their artwork is cold and calculating, yet rendered with a surprising plumpness and vitality through careful attention to line and color.

The exhibition took place in the Baroque chapel of the Istituto Italiano di Cultura a Praga, presented in collaboration with the Fondazione Merz. Tucked into the heart of Malá Strana, amid embassies and the steady flow of tourists bound for Petřín Hill or Prague Castle, the space feels like a quiet interlude. Admission is typically free, and the intimacy of the chapel heightens the encounter with the work.

The Merz’s artwork from the 1980s reveal distinct sensibilities. Mario’s compositions tend toward straight and jagged lines, building depth through layered materials and assertive mark making. His surfaces feel angular, even architectural. Marisa’s works, by contrast, are more fluid. Her contours waver and soften, even as certain lines begin and end abruptly. Where Mario’s images seem to recede inward, Marisa’s appear to rise from the page, pressing gently into the viewer’s space.

Yet Mario’s earlier works from the 1970s introduce an unexpected softness. His depictions of hands swell in bulbous forms, tinged with pale pinks and yellows. The shift from these rounded gestures to the sharper linearity of the 1980s suggests not only personal evolution but also a broader cultural transition, from the diffuse warmth of late 1970s palettes to the harder, metallic edges of 80s punk and electronic dance era. The change reads less as rupture than recalibration.

Marisa’s pages vibrate with fevered pencil strokes. The fineness of her lines creates a paradoxical welcome. The works are intricate, even agitated, yet inviting. Together, the Merzes demonstrate a masterful command of line and color. Their compositions simultaneously deter and beckon, balancing plump, almost tender forms with harsh incisions. A restrained monochrome field might suddenly pulse with a sharp chromatic interruption. The tension holds.

“Premeditated” is an apt descriptor. These are not casual gestures but deliberate constructions. Mario’s early training in medicine and Marisa’s background in ballet seem faintly legible in the discipline of repetition and control. Recurrent strokes carve grooves into the surface, suggesting both material insistence and mental focus. Though the exhibition presents two distinct practices, the dialogue between them is so seamless that the boundaries blur. One could almost mistake the pairing for a single, multifaceted voice.

The show may have closed, but the chapel space continues its programming, offering future exhibitions that promise a similarly thoughtful engagement with history, culture, and form.

images.alt: A pale face surrounded by fine black and red lines on a gold-toned ground.
A copper penny attached to paper covered in dense black marks in the Mario and Marisa Merz exhibition.

title: DOX: BabyDox Workshop
excerpt: Children peered at artworks through masks they had just made, perfectly timed for carnival season.
body:
Children peered at artworks through masks they had just made, perfectly timed for carnival season. It was a playful way to frame how we looked at art while also slowing us down to truly absorb everything Dox has to offer. BabyDox felt both joyful and immersive, and it was ideally suited for my almost four-year-old. Designed for ages two to four, the workshop had plenty for both children and accompanying adults to enjoy.

We took off our coats and shoes and stepped into the room, warmly welcomed by Dox staff. We were invited to create name tags with bright markers arranged on a cushion in the center of the expansive space. Once we settled in, the facilitators encouraged the children to search for puzzle pieces cleverly hidden throughout the room. Each child discovered one and brought it back to the circle, where the fragments assembled into an image of the building as it once appeared. Through this, we learned more about the history of the Dox site we were experiencing firsthand.

Next came mask-making. The children colored their designs, attached them to sticks, and we stepped into the exhibition. We were surrounded by the rich and varied work of Eva Švankmajerová, spanning painting, video, and sculpture. I was reminded of watching Jan Švankmajer’s films decades ago on a bunny-eared television in Kansas, so it felt especially meaningful to encounter those films again here, now in conversation with Švankmajerová’s work at the center. At first the children entered cautiously, then gradually grew more confident, lifting their masks to look closely at the pieces introduced to them.

After exploring the gallery, we returned to the children’s area to create our own art. There were many hands-on options: mixing paints to produce prints, drawing with white crayon and revealing it with broad brushstrokes, and digging through a sensory bin of rice to uncover small treasures like a golden spoon. There were also large foam panels for collaborative fort-building, which quickly became a favorite.

Overall, the experience felt carefully considered for this age group, and we had a truly lovely time. I genuinely appreciate when art spaces welcome children in such creative ways. Starting early with art helps them learn to see the world differently, and this workshop did exactly that.

images.alt: A child looking at a painting through a handmade mask during the BabyDox workshop.

title: Svatopluk Klimeš: Nebezpečná hodina
excerpt: A desiccated bird rising from its own ashes greets the viewer upon entering the exhibition.
body:
A desiccated bird rising from its own ashes greets the viewer upon entering the exhibition. Svatopluk Klimeš’s show, “Nebezpečná hodina” (Dangerous Hour), calls upon nature to guide both medium and process, with fire leaving its signature. The act of burning the page serves as a foreboding warning while simultaneously testing the material’s boundaries. Throughout the gallery, a pervasive sensation of dryness emerges, whiteness like salt, scorched surfaces that create depth, and physical imprints that evoke what has already passed.

At the outset stands “Fenix.” Ash, born from its dinosaur ancestors, harbors a double meaning. It is the creation from one’s origins and a surrender back into primordial matter. The work recalls the ecological fragility of places like California’s Salton Sea, where bird and fish populations have faced dramatic collapse. Nearby, “Modré moře, moře ryb” and “Koně v ledu” extend this visual language. In “Modré moře, moře ryb,” creatures appear stamped onto an arid surface, fish aligned in a single direction while small “x” marks scatter across an open, waterlike field. In “Koně v ledu,” pale horse heads tilt to one side, their eyes marked by burns; they resemble salt pillars more than living animals.

Burning continues to function as a textural device while also carrying hidden iconography across the exhibition. “Povodeň v Terezíně” presents a series of photographs depicting various sites, where a viewer might discern a concealed face with an open mouth or marks that resemble falling rain. An homage to the gallery’s namesake is woven into “Po představení.” Its scorched surface echoes Toyen’s 1943 work “Relâche.” The image feels ominous; a figure hangs upside down yet persists through sheer resilience and determination. The work suggests that endurance is essential, that life is a marathon, and that artists like Klimeš keep a spark alive as a beacon when darkness threatens to overwhelm the masses.

images.alt: Pale horse-head sculptures with burned marks for eyes in Svatopluk Klimeš’s exhibition Nebezpečná hodina.

title: Slávka Krátká at Toyen Gallery
excerpt: Flat cityscapes and seaside escapes line the walls of the Toyen Gallery in Slávka Krátká’s work.
body:
Flat cityscapes and seaside escapes line the walls of the Toyen Gallery in Slávka Krátká’s work. Repetition emerges through the endless rows of windows that rise and fall across the canvas, like the hypnotic infinity of Yayoi Kusama’s dots. The palette feels distinctly Czech: restrained, muted, and only occasionally punctuated by a rare burst of color. It raises the question of whether much Czech art is shaped during long, harsh winters, or whether winter itself, something to be endured and internalized, permanently filters perception, leaving a lingering veil that seeps into the work.

Those subdued tones recall the stained windowsills found in Ivana Lomová’s paintings. Yet Krátká’s surfaces feel flatter, almost deliberately so, lending the work a children’s book quality. There is a sense of wonder that echoes “Dark City,” when the characters finally believe they have escaped the oppressive darkness and reached Shell Beach. What they encounter is vibrant, but also oddly staged, a picturesque façade of what paradise is meant to look like, a carefully constructed dream designed to keep one moving forward.

“Velké koupání” depicts a beach scene populated by waders and boats. From a distance, the figures appear as small bursts of pigment. Up close, their faces resemble the simple, joyful expressions of a child’s drawing, with a classic crescent arch facing upward. There are long-standing debates in art about the legitimacy of childlike visual language, yet artists such as Kandinsky pushed these boundaries decades ago. In the end, it’s the perception of the viewer who determines the validity of art, and that exchange keeps art living.

images.alt: Rows of Czech buildings with blue, red and black rooftops in a painting by Slávka Krátká.

title: Linda Glanc at Toyen Gallery
excerpt: A writhing torso illuminated by deliberate brushstrokes seems caught between desperation and ascent.
body:
A writhing torso illuminated by deliberate brushstrokes seems caught between desperation and ascent. It grasps at a critical moment while a calm, open gesture points upward in quiet hope. To depict strength, pain, and redemption simultaneously through paint is a rare gift, and it is one [@lindaglanc](https://www.instagram.com/lindaglanc/) offers to the world.

The torso appears to lift itself through both its own strength and an unknown force, giving off strong “Stranger Things” vibes. Long, claw-like hands stretch forward as reds and blues collide, creating a scene rooted in nostalgia and voyeurism. We are invited into a private moment of transformation, watching a human-like form suspended between what it was and what it might become. In this way, the work feels deeply relatable.

What may be read as crows circling a dove of peace with a beating red heart forms an unsettling shape. The crows seem to be a menace rather than a helper. Surrounding this tension is a landscape of soft, rolling hills muted by the heaviness of winter. Hope is depicted as possible, but not without a fight.

Several works depict bodies bound with rope, yet the restraint feels chosen rather than imposed. These figures appear complicit in their own confinement, engaging with it as a form of vulnerability or transformation. Blues and reds drip from meticulously rendered bodies, reminding us that humanity is both messy and beautiful.

This is a show worth seeing. The Toyen Gallery is a quiet gem that many overlook. Take the time to view Linda Glanc’s work in person. It may shift how you see not only Czech art, but humanity itself.

Toyen Gallery, Milešovská 846/1, Prague 3  (December 9, 2025)

images.alt: A blue torso and outstretched arm against a purple background in a painting by Linda Glanc.
